title: the Tao: those who know they have enough are rich
hook: the Tao: those who know they have enough are rich
tomorrow: look at something bigger than you today

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: loneliness. Your line: the room is full. Who did you send a thinking-of-you to? Day eighteen.

Think about the last thing you really wanted to buy. The shoes, the phone, the upgrade. Remember how much you wanted it? Now think about how you feel about it today. For most of us, the glow lasts a few days, maybe a few weeks, and then it's just a thing we own, and the wanting has already moved on to the next one. There's a story told about two American novelists, Joseph Heller and Kurt Vonnegut, at a party at a billionaire's house. Vonnegut points out their host made more in a day than Heller's famous book ever earned. And Heller says he has something the billionaire will never have: enough. Today's word is enough.
screen: `THE GLOW LASTS A FEW WEEKS.` → `A PARTY AT A BILLIONAIRE'S HOUSE.` → `SOMETHING HE'LL NEVER HAVE.`

segments.voice: That idea is ancient. The Tao Te Ching, the short Chinese classic traditionally credited to Lao-tzu, has a chapter of paired sayings about strength and knowledge. In the middle of it, in James Legge's 1891 translation: "He who is satisfied with his lot is rich." In the Chinese it's four characters, and the first two mean knowing enough. Not having enough. Knowing it. Richness, in this picture, isn't a number in a bank account. It's a kind of recognition. The Roman Stoic Seneca made the same turn in a letter to a friend: the poor person isn't the one who has too little, but the one who keeps craving more. And the Greek philosopher Epicurus, who's often wrongly remembered as a party animal, lived simply on bread, water and friendship and warned that nothing is enough for the one to whom enough is too little. Modern psychologists have a name for the thing all three were pushing against: the hedonic treadmill. When we get something we wanted, we get used to it, fast, and our sense of normal moves up. So the chase never finishes, because the finish line walks away as we approach it. Knowing enough doesn't mean you stop wanting anything or never improve your life. It means that somewhere, now and then, you step off the treadmill and say the word. This, right here, is enough. The traditions that teach it don't promise it'll make you rich. They say it's what rich actually is.
screen: `SATISFIED WITH HIS LOT IS RICH.` · `THE POOR ONE KEEPS CRAVING MORE.` · `THE HEDONIC TREADMILL.` · `STEP OFF, AND SAY THE WORD.` · then, large: `KNOWING ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let the breath settle. For the next seventy-five seconds, let your eyes or your mind move over what you have right now. Not the whole house, just what's in reach. The chair holding you up. The clothes you're wearing. The breath coming in without being asked. For each one, say inside: enough. Not forever. Just, right now, enough. The bell holds the time.
Enough. Not having it, knowing it. The one thing the billionaire in the story couldn't buy. Eighteenth word.
Your line: enough. Today, the next time you catch yourself wanting the next thing, pause, look at what's already in your hands, and say the word. Day eighteen.

screen: `DAY 18 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: LOOK AT SOMETHING BIGGER THAN YOU TODAY.`

howItsDone: Contentment is practiced in many traditions: Taoists speak of knowing enough, Stoics and Epicureans practiced living simply, and many people keep the habit of pausing to name what they already have.

fork.reveal: in the story, Heller says he has something the host will never have: enough. the Tao Te Ching said it over two thousand years earlier.

original.note: Chinese, zhī zú, from the Tao Te Ching 33: knowing enough, being content. The line reads, word for word, knowing-enough-one rich.

trapdoor: what you thought: having enough money.
what it means: not having enough, knowing it: recognizing that what's here is sufficient.
what a scholar hears: Tao Te Ching 33 reads 知足者富, zhī zú zhě fù: the one who knows enough is rich. Legge renders it satisfied with his lot.

sources.quoted: He who is satisfied with his lot is rich

notes: Legge 1891, ch. 33: confirm exact wording 'He who is satisfied with his lot is rich'.
Seneca Letter 2.6 (Gummere: 'It is not the man who has too little, but the man who craves more, that is poor') paraphrased, since the exact wording wasn't verified.
Epicurus fragment (often numbered Vatican Saying 68 / fr. 473 Usener) paraphrased; confirm attribution. His simple diet (bread and water) is reported by Diogenes Laërtius 10.11.
The Heller–Vonnegut story is told in Vonnegut's 2005 poem (copyrighted); paraphrased only, framed as 'a story told about'.
Index title: 'those who know they have enough are rich' is itself a paraphrase of ch. 33, not Legge's wording.
